content.text: This section justifies the gradient approximation used in ([8](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#S4.E8 "In 4.3 Approximating Noise Gradients for Efficient Steering ‣ 4 StressDream: Steering High-Dimensional Video World Models ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement")). We omit the conditioning variables (𝐨hist,𝐚)(\mathbf{o}^{\text{hist}},\mathbf{a}) for readability. Let the deterministic sampler define the reverse trajectory

where each denoising step follows the update in ([3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#S2.E3 "In 2 Background: Action-conditioned Video World Models ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement")):
For a differentiable criterion 𝒞⁡(𝐱0)\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{x}^{0}), the exact initial-noise gradient is obtained by the chain rule:
where the product is ordered along the reverse denoising trajectory. The Jacobian of each step is
Thus, exact backpropagation requires multiplying by all denoiser Jacobians and storing the full denoising computation graph.

Proportional-Jacobian approximation. Ahn et al. [[3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib31)] empirically observe that the denoiser Jacobian is approximately diagonal and often behaves like a timestep-dependent multiple of the identity. Under the idealized approximation
Substituting this into the exact chain rule yields

This is the approximation used in the main text: instead of differentiating through the sampler, we compute the criterion gradient with respect to the generated clean latent and use it as a scaled proxy for the initial-noise gradient.
Diagonal-Jacobian variant. If the denoiser Jacobian is diagonal but not exactly proportional to the identity,
then the same derivation gives a diagonal preconditioner

The scalar approximation 𝐁≈β​𝐈\mathbf{B}\approx\beta\mathbf{I} is therefore a practical simplification: it assumes the diagonal entries vary slowly enough that their average effect can be absorbed into the optimization step size.

Connection to stop-gradient MSD. Multistep score distillation [[3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib31)] keeps the forward denoising trajectory unchanged but applies a stop-gradient operator to the denoiser outputs during backpropagation. In our notation, the stop-gradient version of one denoising step is

where SG⁡[⋅]\operatorname{SG}[\cdot] is the identity in the forward pass and has zero derivative in the backward pass. Therefore, this removes 𝐉gτ\mathbf{J}^{\tau}\_{g} from the backward pass, leaving only the explicit linear dependence on 𝐱τ\mathbf{x}^{\tau}:
Under the same proportional-Jacobian approximation, both the full-gradient and stop-gradient Jacobian products are scalar multiples of the identity:

Therefore, the stop-gradient gradient and the full sampler gradient differ primarily by timestep-dependent scalar factors. Our approximation uses this same principle, but applies it directly to optimize the initial noise: the clean-latent criterion gradient is used as a proxy direction for the initial-noise gradient, with the unknown scalar absorbed into β\beta and the learning rate.

Efficacy of Gradient Approximation for Noise Optimization. The noise-gradient approximation enables efficient gradient-based steering without backpropagating through the iterative denoising process of large-scale video diffusion models. However, it relies on the assumption that the Jacobian of the diffusion sampler is approximately diagonal [[3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib31)]. Indeed, prior work on noise optimization for text-to-image generation often relies on one-step distilled generators to make noise optimization tractable without differentiating through the full iterative sampling process.

We therefore empirically evaluate whether this approximation provides a useful gradient signal in the initial-noise space for generating high-reward samples in the output space. Fig. [12](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#A2.F12 "Figure 12 ‣ B.4 Score-Distillation for Approximating Initial-Noise Gradients ‣ Appendix B Inference-time Steering of Video World Models ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement") shows the average VLM score during noise optimization for steering Vista [[38](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib94)] generations in Sec. [6.1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#S6.SS1 "6.1 Robust Policy Evaluation using State-of-the-Art Video World Models ‣ 6 Experiments: Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement"). The score increases throughout optimization, indicating that the approximate gradient can improve the output-space VLM objective by updating only the initial noise. On an H100 GPU with 8080GB VRAM, computing the full gradient through the denoising trajectory is impractical even with gradient checkpointing [[21](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib116)], whereas the proposed approximation makes the optimization feasible.

For Ctrl-World [[42](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib108)], where the full noise gradient can be computed on an H100 GPU using gradient checkpointing [[21](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib116)], we compare noise optimization with and without the gradient approximation. Fig. [13](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#A2.F13 "Figure 13 ‣ B.4 Score-Distillation for Approximating Initial-Noise Gradients ‣ Appendix B Inference-time Steering of Video World Models ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement") shows that the approximate gradient successfully increases the VLM score, whereas optimization with the full gradient fails to improve it. We hypothesize two possible causes. First, backpropagating through 5050 denoising steps may lead to inaccurate or vanishing gradients due to finite-precision computation. Second, while the VLM gradient is computed in the video space with relatively high numerical precision, the denoising process is typically run in lower precision due to memory constraints, which may further degrade gradient quality.

We summarize the overall procedure of StressDream in Algorithm [1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#algorithm1 "In B.5 Implementation Details ‣ Appendix B Inference-time Steering of Video World Models ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement"). To improve optimization stability, we use both global gradient-norm clipping and per-coordinate gradient clipping. We additionally monitor the Euclidean norm of the noise and project it back to the typical shell, with norm D\sqrt{D}, whenever it deviates by more than 3.03.0. This threshold is conservative: the standard deviation of the Gaussian norm is approximately 0.7070.707 in high dimensions, as shown in Corollary [2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#Thmcorollary2 "Corollary 2 (Dimension-independent width of the Gaussian shell). ‣ B.2 Concentration of Gaussian Typical Set Regularizers ‣ Appendix B Inference-time Steering of Video World Models ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement"), so the interval contains more than 99.99%99.99\% of typical Gaussian samples. In addition, we omit momentum in the optimizer, since accumulated updates can easily push the noise outside the typical set.

We analyze the time complexity of the proposed world model steering algorithm. Let 𝒯denoise\mathcal{T}\_{\mathrm{denoise}} denote the cost of one denoising step and KK the number of denoising steps used by the video world model. A single deterministic generation costs 𝒯gen=K×𝒯denoise.\mathcal{T}\_{\mathrm{gen}}=K\times\mathcal{T}\_{\mathrm{denoise}}. Let 𝒯verifier\mathcal{T}\_{\mathrm{verifier}} denote the cost of evaluating the verifier, such as a VLM-based criterion, on a generated video.

Approx. (Sec.[4.3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#S4.SS3 "4.3 Approximating Noise Gradients for Efficient Steering ‣ 4 StressDream: Steering High-Dimensional Video World Models ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement")) | N×(2​K×𝒯denoise+2​𝒯verifier)N\times\left(2K\times\mathcal{T}\_{\mathrm{denoise}}+2\,\mathcal{T}\_{\mathrm{verifier}}\right) |

Table [1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#A2.T1 "Table 1 ‣ B.6 Time Complexity ‣ Appendix B Inference-time Steering of Video World Models ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement") compares nominal generation, Best-of-NN sampling, and StressDream under the same budget of NN sampled candidates or steering iterations. Compared to Best-of-NN sampling, StressDream adds the cost of computing a verifier gradient at each steering iteration. With the gradient approximation in Sec. [4.3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#S4.SS3 "4.3 Approximating Noise Gradients for Efficient Steering ‣ 4 StressDream: Steering High-Dimensional Video World Models ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement"), however, StressDream avoids backpropagating through the full denoising trajectory, so the additional cost is mainly the backward pass through the verifier, represented by the second 𝒯verifier\mathcal{T}\_{\mathrm{verifier}} term. Without this approximation, differentiating through the KK-step sampler adds a backward pass through the denoising trajectory, substantially increasing both computation and memory.

In practice, using Vista [[38](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib94)] with K=50K=50 denoising steps on a single H100 GPU, a single generation takes approximately 11–22 minutes, while noise optimization with N=20N=20 iterations takes about 3030 minutes. Since the dominant cost comes from video generation, the runtime of StressDream is expected to improve with faster video world models, such as shortcut [[37](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib15), [47](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib85)] models.

Video World Model. We implement a video world model for the Naughty Dubins car environment using a smaller-scale SVD-style latent diffusion architecture [[14](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib96)] trained with the EDM formulation [[59](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib58)]. Following [98](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib8), each observation is a rendered 128×128×3128\times 128\times 3 RGB image showing the vehicle and the circular failure set at the center of the environment.

| | | | --- | --- | | World Model Hyperparameter | Value | | Image Resolution | 128×128×3128\times 128\times 3 | | Latent Dimension | 1024 | | Prediction Horizon HH | 1 | | Action Dimension | 1 (continuous) | | VAE Base Channels | 32 | | VAE Latent Channels | 4 | | Denoiser Hidden Dims. | [32, 64, 128] | | Denoising Steps | 5 | | σmin\sigma\_{\min}, σmax\sigma\_{\max} | 0.002, 80.0 | | EDM ρ\rho | 7 | | Batch Size | 128 | | Training Epochs | 100 | | Learning Rate | 1×10−41\times 10^{-4} |

We train the model on an offline dataset of observation–action trajectories generated from random initial states and random actions, with each trajectory annotated by the ground-truth safety margin. Each trajectory terminates after T=100T=100 timesteps or earlier if the ground-truth xx- or yy-position leaves the environment bounds [−1.5​m,1.5​m][-1.5\,\mathrm{m},1.5\,\mathrm{m}]. The encoder maps observations ot∈ℝH×W×Co\_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W\times C} to latent representations zt∈ℝH/8×W/8×4z\_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{H/8\times W/8\times 4}, which are decoded back to RGB observations using a lightweight decoder. We train the latent autoencoder with a reconstruction objective and train the failure-margin predictor ℓθ\ell\_{\theta} using an L2L\_{2} regression loss against the ground-truth safety margin. We then train the latent diffusion transition model fθf\_{\theta} to generate the next latent state conditioned on the current latent state and action. In our experiments, we use one-step latent prediction (H=1)(H=1), yielding a latent and noise dimension of 10241024. At inference time, we use an Euler sampler with 55 denoising steps. The world-model hyperparameters are summarized in Tables [2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#A3.T2 "Table 2 ‣ C.1 Implementation Details ‣ Appendix C Naughty Dubins Car ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement").

Evaluation Setup. We evaluate steering on autoregressive rollouts of the video world model. Each rollout starts from the initial image of an evaluation trajectory and is conditioned on the corresponding action sequence. We assign a ground-truth label to each evaluation trajectory using Monte Carlo rollouts of the true uncertain dynamics in ([9](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#S5.E9 "In 5 Case Study: Steering Dubins Car Video World Model ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement")). For each initial state and action sequence, we sample 10,00010{,}000 ground-truth trajectories. We label the trajectory as positive if at least one sampled trajectory enters the failure set, indicating that failure is possible.

We label it as negative if none of the sampled trajectories enter the failure set. This allows us to evaluate whether pessimistic steering identifies genuinely failure-prone trajectories while avoiding spurious failures on trajectories that are effectively safe under the true dynamics. We steer the generated rollout using the hyperparameters in Table [3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#A3.T3 "Table 3 ‣ C.1 Implementation Details ‣ Appendix C Naughty Dubins Car ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement"). Since this setup is small-scale, we use the full gradient without the approximation. This allows us to directly evaluate the effect of optimizing the initial noise and the proposed regularizers without introducing additional approximation error from the gradient estimator.

Baseline: Classifier Guidance. We also compare against classifier guidance [[26](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib17), [69](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib18)], which modifies the denoising process at each diffusion step using the gradient of the failure criterion. In the world-model setting, however, such guidance is difficult to apply directly. The failure predictor ℓθ\ell\_{\theta} is trained on clean latent states, not on noisy intermediate diffusion states. Therefore, evaluating ℓθ\ell\_{\theta} directly on ztτz\_{t}^{\tau} can provide unreliable gradients, while exact guidance would require backpropagating through the denoiser at every denoising step.

To make classifier guidance tractable, we use a one-step clean-latent approximation [[69](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib18)]. Given a noisy latent zt+1τz\_{t+1}^{\tau}, we estimate the corresponding clean latent by inverting the forward diffusion path:
The guidance gradient is then computed on this approximately clean latent:

which avoids backpropagating through the denoising network, but it can introduce bias because the one-step clean prediction may be misaligned with the final generated latent after the full denoising trajectory. This issue is particularly pronounced in action-conditioned world models, where small guidance errors can push the generation toward high-failure latents that are inconsistent with the conditioning action sequence or the learned dynamics.

Results: Pessimistic Steering. Fig. [14](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#A3.F14 "Figure 14 ‣ C.1 Implementation Details ‣ Appendix C Naughty Dubins Car ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement") reports the average minimum safety score over imagined trajectories for the experiments in Sec. [5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#S5 "5 Case Study: Steering Dubins Car Video World Model ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement"). StressDream effectively steers imaginations toward lower safety scores that closely match the minimum achievable safety scores of the ground-truth system, suggesting that WM imaginations can provide meaningful signals for policy evaluation. In contrast, CG and StressDream without the plausibility objective predict implausibly low safety scores, indicating that they can over-steer generations beyond plausible outcomes.

While Sec. [5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#S5 "5 Case Study: Steering Dubins Car Video World Model ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement") focuses on pessimistic steering to detect potential entries into the failure set, we also ablate the opposite direction by performing optimistic steering. Specifically, we change the sign of the steering objective so that optimization seeks imaginations with higher safety scores. Fig. [15](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#A3.F15 "Figure 15 ‣ C.2 Ablation: Optimistic Steering ‣ Appendix C Naughty Dubins Car ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement") shows the resulting maximum safety score for each imagined trajectory, together with the maximum safety score achievable under the ground-truth stochastic dynamics as a horizontal reference line. The results are consistent with the findings in Sec. [5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#S5 "5 Case Study: Steering Dubins Car Video World Model ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement"): StressDream can steer the world model effectively, here toward optimistic outcomes, while keeping the generated trajectories plausibly bounded by the ground-truth uncertainty. In contrast, removing the regularizers or using classifier guidance can also increase the imagined safety score, but often produces overly optimistic generations that exceed what is plausible under the ground-truth system dynamics.

children.heading: C.3 Ablation: Impact of plausibility objective

content.text: We ablate the impact of the regularizers in Sec. [4.2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#S4.SS2 "4.2 Plausibility Objective: Keeping High-dimensional Noise in the Typical Set ‣ 4 StressDream: Steering High-Dimensional Video World Models ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement") on keeping generations plausible, or in-distribution. Unlike video world models trained on internet-scale data, this controlled setting gives us tractable access to the training distribution, allowing us to directly inspect whether steering keeps generations consistent with the training-time distribution. We report typicality scores of the optimized initial noise, including the chi-square log-probability of the squared noise norm, the isotropy regularizer value, and the spectral-whiteness regularizer value. We also remove each regularizer individually to evaluate its contribution.

Empirical Density Estimation. We additionally evaluate whether the generated samples themselves remain in-distribution by fitting a flow-matching density surrogate in the latent observation space [[124](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib2)]. Let z=ℰθ​(o)z=\mathcal{E}\_{\theta}(o) denote the latent representation of an observation from the training dataset. We train a flow-matching vector field qψq\_{\psi} that transports training latents to standard Gaussian noise. Specifically, for w∼𝒩⁡(0,𝐈)w\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{I}) and τ∈[0,1]\tau\in[0,1], define the linear interpolation
The vector field is trained to predict the displacement toward the Gaussian endpoint:
Given a generated latent z^t\hat{z}\_{t}, we estimate its corresponding Gaussian endpoint with a one-step prediction from τ=0\tau=0:

If z^t\hat{z}\_{t} is in-distribution, then w^t\widehat{w}\_{t} should be close to a sample from 𝒩⁡(0,𝐈)\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{I}). Since the Gaussian log-density is proportional to −‖w^t‖22-\|\widehat{w}\_{t}\|\_{2}^{2}, we use

as the latent OOD score. A higher score indicates that the generated latent is farther from the distribution of encoded in-distribution observations. This density-based OOD score complements the noise-space regularizers by checking whether the resulting generated samples, not only the optimized initial noise, remain plausible.

Results. Norm concentration is measured by the minimum chi-square log-probability of the noise norm, where higher values indicate more typical Gaussian noise. Isotropy and spectral whiteness are regularizer values, where lower values are better.

StressDream with all regularizers keeps the noise statistics close to nominal generation while maintaining a low OOD score. In contrast, steering without regularization produces highly atypical noise and substantially larger OOD scores, suggesting that the optimized generations leave the training distribution. Classifier guidance keeps the initial noise statistics close to nominal because it modifies the denoising trajectory rather than the initial noise, but it still increases the OOD score, indicating that path-level guidance can push generated samples toward implausible regions. Removing individual regularizers also increases the OOD score compared to using all regularizers, highlighting the importance of combining norm concentration, isotropy, and spectral whiteness.

Hyperparameters. The action input is an 88-dimensional vector representing the top-down future ego trajectory as four future waypoints. For Ctrl-World [[42](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib108)]22 2 <https://github.com/Robert-gyj/Ctrl-World>, videos are subsampled to 55Hz, and the action input consists of joint-position and gripper commands. Since each prediction generates 55 future frames, the action dimension is 40=8×H40=8\times H. To imagine longer manipulation trajectories, we use autoregressive generation, where the last generated frame is used as the initial conditioning frame for the next prediction window.

Fine-tuning. We find that fine-tuning the base checkpoints of the video world models is important for plausibly imagining task-relevant rare events, such as collisions or coffee-bean spills, and for aligning the train- and test-time distributions to improve video quality. While the base models are trained on diverse datasets, such as nuScenes [[16](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib59)] or DROID [[62](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib9)], their generated futures can suffer from degraded dynamics accuracy and visual quality when evaluated on our specific scenarios. We therefore fine-tune each video world model for a small number of iterations on task-relevant data.

| Task | Block Stack | Knife Put | Stacked Utensil Pick | Coffee Bean Pour | Open Coffee Bag | Open Candy Bag | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | # Trajectories | 250250 | 170170 | 200200 | 100100 | 170170 | 150150 |

For autonomous driving, we fine-tune the video world model using a subset of the PhysicalAI-Autonomous-Vehicles (PAI-AV) dataset [[86](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib62)], nuScenes [[16](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib59)], and the Nexar Collision Prediction Dataset [[81](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib63)]. We train for 13,75013{,}750 iterations with a batch size of 256256. For manipulation, we fine-tune Ctrl-World using teleoperation trajectories that include both successful and failure cases. We use a learning rate of 1×10−61\times 10^{-6}, a batch size of 6464, and train for 10,00010{,}000 iterations. Table [7](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#A4.T7 "Table 7 ‣ D.1 Video World Models ‣ Appendix D Experiment Details ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement") summarizes the number of teleoperation trajectories used for each manipulation task.

We describe the manipulation task setups, the criteria used to determine success or failure, and the language prompts used for steering the generated futures. Visual examples of the task setups are shown in Fig. [6](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#S6.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ 6.2 Policy Improvement with Steered Video World Model Imaginations ‣ 6 Experiments: Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement") and on the [project website](https://stressdream.github.io/).

Block Stack. Two Jenga blocks, one orange and one blue, are placed on the table. The robot is tasked with stacking the orange block on top of the blue block. A trajectory is considered a success if the orange block remains on top of the blue block, and a failure if the robot fails to stack the block or if the orange block falls off after stacking. VLM prompt: Are the two blocks stacked? Respond with a single word: Yes or No.

Knife Put. A lightweight plastic bowl and a knife are placed on the table. The robot is tasked with picking up the knife and placing it inside the bowl without causing either object to fall. This task is challenging because the knife has an uneven center of mass and a complex shape, while the lightweight bowl can easily tip over. A trajectory is considered a success if the knife is placed inside the bowl and remains there, and a failure if the knife falls out or the bowl tips over. VLM prompt: Is the knife placed inside of the blue bowl without falling out? Respond with a single word: Yes or No.

Stacked Utensil Pick. A blue knife and a red spoon are overlapped on a green plate, with the red spoon placed on top of the blue knife. The robot is instructed to pick up the blue knife while keeping the red spoon on the plate. A trajectory is considered a success if the blue knife is successfully picked up and the spoon remains on the plate, and a failure if the blue knife is not picked up or if the spoon falls off the plate. The robot should therefore remove the lower utensil while safely leaving the upper utensil on the plate. VLM prompt: Is the red spoon in the green plate? Respond with a single word: Yes or No.

Coffee Bean Pour. A bowl is on top of a coffee scale, and a cup contains coffee beans. The robot is tasked with pouring the coffee beans from the cup into the bowl on the scale. A trajectory is considered a success if the coffee beans are poured into the bowl without spilling, and a failure if any coffee beans spill onto the table. VLM prompt: Is the coffee bean spilled on the table? Respond with a single word: Yes or No.

Open Coffee Bag. An open coffee bag with a variable and partially unobservable amount of coffee beans inside is on the table, along with a container. The robot is instructed to place the coffee bag inside the container. A trajectory is considered a failure if any coffee beans spill out of the bag, either into the container or onto the table. Thus, the robot must avoid spilling while lifting, carrying, and placing the bag into the container. VLM prompt: Is the coffee bean spilled? Respond with a single word: Yes or No.

Open Candy Bag. An open gummy bear candy bag is on the table, and the robot is instructed to place it inside the container without spilling. Compared to coffee beans, gummy bears are stickier and heavier, creating a smaller risk of spilling out of the bag. A trajectory is considered a success if the gummy bears remain inside the bag, and a failure if any gummy bears spill out. VLM prompt: Does candy spill from an open bag? Respond with a single word: Yes or No.

children.heading: D.3 Autonomous Driving: Evaluation Data Curation

content.text: To evaluate steering for autonomous driving video world models, we curate an evaluation set from the PAI-AV dataset [[86](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib62)]. We focus on scenarios in which the future evolution is uncertain or interaction-dependent, such as pedestrian crossing, vehicle merging, traffic-light changes, and stop-sign behavior. Table [8](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#A4.T8 "Table 8 ‣ D.3 Autonomous Driving: Evaluation Data Curation ‣ Appendix D Experiment Details ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement") summarizes the event categories and the verifier prompts used for Qwen-VL [[8](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib51)] and X-CLIP [[76](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib64)]. For X-CLIP, the first text description is treated as the positive event description, while the remaining descriptions are used as negative alternatives.

To retrieve candidate clips from the large-scale dataset, we first extract VLM reasoning traces from Alpamayo-R1 [[118](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib61)] on PAI-AV clips. We then embed these traces using Sentence-BERT [[93](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib60)] and retrieve the top-kk clips whose embeddings are most similar to text descriptions of each event category. Human annotators then verify whether the target event occurs in each retrieved clip and label the event occurrence time. Since the video world model generates 2.52.5s futures, we select the frame 2.52.5s before the annotated event time as the initial observation for evaluation. We similarly curate an evaluation set of 200200 collision clips from the Nexar Collision Prediction Dataset [[81](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib63)] by randomly sampling from the provided collision annotations.

Autonomous Driving. To evaluate steering, we use held-out metrics that are not used during optimization. This is important because a steered generation can increase the optimization score without producing a meaningful or plausible change in the video. We therefore evaluate two complementary aspects: (i) target alignment, i.e., whether the generated video clearly depicts the target event described by the text prompt, and (ii) plausibility, i.e., whether the generated video remains physically reasonable and free from severe visual artifacts that indicate out-of-distribution generation.

For autonomous driving, we adopt WorldModelBench (WMB) [[68](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib98)], which evaluates video world-model generations using both text-prompt alignment and video-quality criteria. We use WMB because it includes driving data in its evaluation distribution and, empirically, provides meaningful scores for whether generated driving videos both match the target prompt and remain visually plausible. WMB reports three scores: instruction following (0​–​3)(0\text{--}3), physics adherence (0​–​5)(0\text{--}5), and commonsense consistency (0​–​2)(0\text{--}2). We use the instruction-following score to measure target alignment, and use physics adherence and commonsense consistency as proxies for generation plausibility.

In addition, we report a target-alignment score from an external VLM judge. This judge is used only for evaluation and is not used during steering. We use the following prompt template with Gemini [[107](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib66)] to obtain a 0​–​100\text{--}10 alignment score:

You are an expert evaluator of autonomous driving world models. Your ONLY task is to judge how well the video follows the text instruction. Ignore visual quality issues such as blur, flickering, warping, or low resolution: these are expected artifacts of world-model generation and must NOT affect your score.
10: The video is aligned with the text description clearly and completely.
7-9: The video is aligned with the text description but with minor deviations (e.g., slightly wrong direction or timing).
4-6: The video is vaguely related to the text description, but the specific action does not happen.
1-3: The video is completely unrelated to the text description.
0: The video content is completely unrelated to the text description.

Robotic Manipulation. We use human evaluation to determine whether each generated trajectory corresponds to task success or failure. We additionally report scores from Robometer [[71](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib65)], a general-purpose robotic reward model. However, we rely on human evaluation as the primary metric for a more accurate assessment of generated trajectories, since reward models provide continuous scores and require prompt engineering to infer task success.

We fine-tune the π0.5\pi\_{0.5}-droid policy33 3 <https://github.com/Physical-Intelligence/openpi> using 4040 expert trajectories per task with a weighted flow-matching objective [[41](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib109)]. After steering the imagined rollout of each trajectory toward task failure, we assign a weight of 1.01.0 to trajectories classified as successful and a weight of 0.10.1 to trajectories steered to failure. We use two camera views, consisting of a wrist camera and one third-person camera. The weights are applied both to the fine-tuning loss and to dataset sampling. We use joint-position actions for fine-tuning, although the base policy was originally trained with joint-velocity actions, because our controller [[131](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib100)] does not support joint-velocity control. We fine-tune the pretrained checkpoint for 1010k steps on a single H100 GPU. At inference time, we use an open-loop action horizon of 1616. We found that training a diffusion policy [[22](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib101)] from scratch performs poorly in this setting, likely due to the contact-rich nature of our tasks and the limited size of the fine-tuning dataset. In contrast, fine-tuning π0.5\pi\_{0.5}-droid produces substantially better behavior and clearly imitates the expert demonstrations after fine-tuning.

children.heading: E.1 Robust Policy Evaluation via Video World Model Steering

content.text: In this section, we provide additional results for Sec. [6.1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#S6.SS1 "6.1 Robust Policy Evaluation using State-of-the-Art Video World Models ‣ 6 Experiments: Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement"). The evaluation focuses on steering video world-model generations toward text-defined failure events in each scene, enabling robust evaluation of policy-proposed action sequences through pessimistic world-model imaginations. We measure both target alignment, i.e., how well the generated videos match the failure prompt, and plausibility, i.e., whether the generations remain visually and physically reasonable. Full results, including videos and interactive demos, are available on the [project website](https://stressdream.github.io/).

Robust Policy Evaluation with Pessimistic Imaginations. Fig. [16](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#A5.F16 "Figure 16 ‣ E.1 Robust Policy Evaluation via Video World Model Steering ‣ Appendix E Additional Results ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement") shows additional results for the inner optimization in ([4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#S3.E4 "In 3 Setup: Policy Evaluation and Improvement with Video World Models ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement")) on robotic manipulation tasks. For the same observation history and action sequence, nominal imaginations often do not predict failure events, whereas StressDream generates plausible task-failure futures from the same input. This enables robust policy evaluation using the video world model by detecting possible failures through synthetic trajectories, without requiring repeated hardware rollouts. In contrast, nominal generation may miss such failures because it can sample non-failing futures even when failure is possible. Similarly, Fig. [17](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#A5.F17 "Figure 17 ‣ E.1 Robust Policy Evaluation via Video World Model Steering ‣ Appendix E Additional Results ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement") shows that, across different candidate action sequences, StressDream with pessimistic steering can reveal potential failures or safety-critical events in the imagined futures, while robust action sequences remain safe even under pessimistic imagination. This supports robust evaluation and action selection by using the video world model as a predictive model for planning and control.

Detailed Results: Driving Video World Model. Fig. [18](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#A5.F18 "Figure 18 ‣ E.1 Robust Policy Evaluation via Video World Model Steering ‣ Appendix E Additional Results ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement") shows the full quantitative results for driving world-model [[38](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib94)] steering, evaluated with WorldModelBench (WMB) [[68](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib98)] and Gemini-3.0 [[107](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib66)]. The top two plots measure target alignment between the generated videos and the steering text prompts, while the bottom two plots report WMB video-quality metrics. Across both alignment metrics, StressDream with noise optimization more effectively increases target-event alignment scores than the baselines with random generation, indicating that the proposed steering procedure reliably guides video world-model generation toward the desired events. At the same time, the proposed typical set constraint helps maintain plausibility: although video quality slightly decreases at later optimization steps, ours consistently preserves better quality in both common sense scores and physical laws scores than steering without regularization.

Typical Set Constraints Preserve Plausibility of Steered Video Generations. We have evaluated the plausibility of steered generations on VLM-based scores, such as the commonsense and physical-law scores in WorldModelBench [[68](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib98)]. To further assess the role of the plausibility objective in Sec. [4.2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#S4.SS2 "4.2 Plausibility Objective: Keeping High-dimensional Noise in the Typical Set ‣ 4 StressDream: Steering High-Dimensional Video World Models ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement"), we additionally evaluate generated driving videos using WorldLens [[72](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib99)]. We focus on generation-quality metrics that assess whether generated videos are visually realistic, temporally stable, and semantically consistent, without requiring multi-view images or ground-truth labels. Unlike VLM-based scores, these metrics are computed from analytic feature-based measures44 4 WorldLens also introduces a learned video score trained from large-scale human annotations of world realism, physical plausibility, and behavioral safety; however, since this model is not yet released..

Specifically, we evaluate Subject Consistency, Depth Discrepancy, and Temporal Consistency. Subject Consistency uses DINO features [[87](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib91)] to measure whether dynamic subjects maintain consistent texture, shape, and structure over time. Depth Discrepancy measures the temporal stability of depth representations inferred from generated videos using DepthAnything [[20](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib93)]. Temporal Consistency measures frame-to-frame stability in a learned appearance space using CLIP encodings [[92](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib92)]. We refer readers to the appendix of WorldLens [[72](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib99)] for detailed metric definitions. Fig. [19](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#A5.F19 "Figure 19 ‣ E.1 Robust Policy Evaluation via Video World Model Steering ‣ Appendix E Additional Results ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement") shows the WorldLens generation-quality scores for driving world-model generations. Consistent with the WMB video-quality metrics, generation quality tends to degrade at later noise-optimization steps. However, using the proposed typical set constraints substantially mitigates this degradation, preserving subject consistency, depth stability, and temporal consistency compared to steering without regularization.

Detailed Results: Failure Detection in Robotic Manipulation. Fig. [21](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#A5.F21 "Figure 21 ‣ E.1 Robust Policy Evaluation via Video World Model Steering ‣ Appendix E Additional Results ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement") reports task-wise failure-detection results for robotic manipulation video world models. Steering is performed using Qwen3-VL [[9](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib50)] scores computed from task-failure prompts, while the detection results are evaluated against trajectory-level success and failure labels from the dataset. Across tasks, StressDream detects substantially more failure-prone trajectories than nominal generation or Best-of-NN sampling.

Fig. [21](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#A5.F21 "Figure 21 ‣ E.1 Robust Policy Evaluation via Video World Model Steering ‣ Appendix E Additional Results ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement") also shows that StressDream sometimes predicts failures for trajectories labeled as non-failure in the dataset. This should not be interpreted strictly as a false-positive rate: a trajectory that succeeded during data collection may still be risky under unobserved factors in a partially observable setting. Qualitatively, many of these flagged trajectories correspond to risky behaviors, suggesting that pessimistic imagination provides a more robust way of evaluating policies. At the same time, StressDream does not flag all non-failure trajectories as failures, indicating that the method can still identify robust trajectories that remain safe even under pessimistic world-model imagination. These robust trajectories can then be prioritized for policy improvement, rather than relying on demonstrations that may have succeeded only by chance.

children.heading: E.2 StressDream Can Effectively Discover Rare, Long-Tailed Events

content.text: Our main experiments evaluate whether StressDream can generate videos that satisfy an inference-time specification while preserving plausibility more effectively than random sampling. This is particularly important for video world models, which operate in high-dimensional spaces where targeted generation is difficult: rare events often occupy complex, multimodal, and low-probability regions of the generative distribution, making random sampling highly sample-inefficient. In this section, we ask a complementary question: can StressDream effectively discover rare events in the target distribution by optimizing the initial noise with VLM guidance?

To evaluate this, we sample 55 evaluation examples from long-tailed driving events in the evaluation set, including pedestrian crossing, traffic-light change, and collision. As a baseline, we generate 4040 random samples and report the best result among them, while StressDream performs 2020 optimization steps. We evaluate target alignment scores of generated videos using Gemini-3.0 [[107](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib66)]. Fig. [22](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#A5.F22 "Figure 22 ‣ E.2 StressDream Can Effectively Discover Rare, Long-Tailed Events ‣ Appendix E Additional Results ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement") shows that StressDream is more effective at discovering rare events than random sampling. Even with 4040 samples, Best-of-NN sampling does not match the target-alignment score achieved by StressDream. This suggests that first-order optimization in the high-dimensional noise space can discover rare, long-tailed events more efficiently than zeroth-order search through random sampling.

children.heading: E.3 StressDream Steers into Plausible Outcomes Only

content.text: We further elaborate on the experiments in Sec. [6.1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#S6.SS1 "6.1 Robust Policy Evaluation using State-of-the-Art Video World Models ‣ 6 Experiments: Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement") by examining whether steered generations remain grounded in plausible outcomes of the world model. In particular, we compare a driving world model fine-tuned with collision data against the base model without such fine-tuning. As shown in Fig. [5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#S6.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 6.1 Robust Policy Evaluation using State-of-the-Art Video World Models ‣ 6 Experiments: Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement"), the base model yields low text–video alignment scores for collision events, even compared to random sampling from the collision-fine-tuned model, because collisions are not represented in its predictive distribution and therefore cannot be plausibly imagined.

Fig. [23](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#A5.F23 "Figure 23 ‣ E.3 StressDream Steers into Plausible Outcomes Only ‣ Appendix E Additional Results ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement") shows a qualitative example of imagination near a collision event using the base model and the collision-fine-tuned model. The base model fails to imagine the collision and instead hallucinates the other vehicle disappearing from the scene. In contrast, the fine-tuned model, whose predictive distribution includes collision events, correctly imagines the collision. This supports our claim that when the optimized noise remains close to the Gaussian prior, steering produces samples that are still supported by the world model distribution, rather than arbitrary hallucinations. In this sense, noise optimization differs from simply forcing inference-time alignment through a classifier or a fine-tuning objective, which can more easily push the generation off-manifold.

Similarly, Fig. [24](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#A5.F24 "Figure 24 ‣ E.3 StressDream Steers into Plausible Outcomes Only ‣ Appendix E Additional Results ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement") shows an example of steering a driving WM generation so that the distance between the ego vehicle and the lead vehicle decreases. In the initial generation, the lead vehicle moves forward, roughly maintaining its distance from the ego vehicle. In the steered generation, the lead vehicle instead remains stopped while the ego vehicle continues moving, causing the distance to decrease. Although the distance could be reduced even further if the lead vehicle moved backward, such behavior is highly implausible in a normal driving scenario. Accordingly, the steered generation chooses the plausible outcome of the lead vehicle stopping, rather than the implausible outcome of it reversing. By contrast, when steering is performed without the plausibility objective, the generation hallucinates unrealistic artifacts, such as the distorted backward motion of vehicle shapes.

Fig. [25](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#A5.F25 "Figure 25 ‣ E.4 Robust Policy Improvement ‣ Appendix E Additional Results ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement") reports the task-wise success rates of the π0.5\pi\_{0.5}-droid policy fine-tuned with video world-model imaginations (Sec. [6.2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#S6.SS2 "6.2 Policy Improvement with Steered Video World Model Imaginations ‣ 6 Experiments: Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement")). Across all tasks, the Robust π0.5FT\pi\_{0.5}^{\mathrm{FT}} policy achieves higher success rates than the Nominal π0.5FT\pi\_{0.5}^{\mathrm{FT}} policy. This suggests that pessimistic imaginations help identify and downweight failure-prone demonstrations, thereby promoting actions that remain successful.

Suboptimality of Noise Optimization. While StressDream provides a practical instantiation of steering video WM imaginations via gradient-based noise optimization, the optimized noise may still be suboptimal. The optimization in StressDream should be viewed as a local refinement of the initial noise rather than a global search over all possible futures. Exhaustively searching the high-dimensional noise space is infeasible: if ϵ,ϵ′​∼i.i.d.​𝒩​(𝟎,𝐈D)\bm{\epsilon},\bm{\epsilon}^{\prime}\overset{\mathrm{i.i.d.}}{\sim}\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}\_{D}), then ϵ−ϵ′∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,2​𝐈D)\bm{\epsilon}-\bm{\epsilon}^{\prime}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},2\mathbf{I}\_{D}), so ‖ϵ−ϵ′‖22/2∼χD2\|\bm{\epsilon}-\bm{\epsilon}^{\prime}\|\_{2}^{2}/2\sim\chi\_{D}^{2}, and therefore ‖ϵ−ϵ′‖2\|\bm{\epsilon}-\bm{\epsilon}^{\prime}\|\_{2} concentrates around 2​D\sqrt{2D}. In contrast, the average L2L\_{2} distance between the initial and optimized noises in our experiments is far smaller, indicating that StressDream performs local refinement rather than global exploration. The typical-set constraints make gradient updates reliable mainly within a moderate local region; overly large updates can push the noise OOD and make generations implausible. A natural extension is to combine Best-of-NN-style search with gradient-based refinement [[75](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib124), [126](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib23)], or to learn a value function [[54](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib28)] to guide denoising. Finally, for video WMs that require autoregressive rollouts, later generations condition on previously generated futures. The optimal solution would therefore require jointly optimizing a sequence of noises across rollout segments, but the current implementation solves it sequentially.

Preserving Plausibility. StressDream preserves plausibility by regularizing the optimized noise, encouraging it to remain in the typical set of the high-dimensional Gaussian. However, our notion of plausibility is defined with respect to the learned WM distribution: it assumes that generations from Gaussian noise are plausible under the WM. Thus, StressDream can keep steering within the outcomes the WM supports, but it cannot correct a base WM that already produces physically implausible generations. One could incorporate video-quality or physical-consistency metrics as part of the steering objective [[89](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib40), [34](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib20), [33](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib29)], to explicitly bias generations toward higher-quality imaginations. Conversely, StressDream also cannot imagine outcomes that may be plausible in the real world but are absent from the WM distribution. This highlights the importance of training WMs on diverse interaction data, including failures and rare outcomes, rather than success-only data [[62](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib9)], so that their predictive distributions can support policy evaluation and improvement.

Computational Inefficiency. Although StressDream is sample-efficient for generating plausible target outcomes compared to random sampling by leveraging dense VLM gradients, its runtime is still primarily bottlenecked by video WM generation, which can take several minutes per imagination with current models [[38](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib94), [50](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib95), [42](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib108), [1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib103)]. Inference-time steering methods for text-to-image generation often reduce this cost with step-distilled or shortcut models that generate samples in one or a few denoising steps, making both noise optimization and gradient computation more tractable [[34](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib20), [33](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib29)]. Our method is orthogonal to these advances: as video WMs become faster, StressDream directly benefits from improved sampling efficiency, and shortcut models may enable more accurate gradient computations without relying on the current approximation. Another promising direction is to amortize the iterative optimization by learning a noise generator for fixed target outcomes, similar to [33](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib29), [113](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib35), but enforcing the typical-set constraints in high-dimensional initial noise space remains challenging. Lastly, StressDream incurs additional overhead from backpropagating through the criterion function, making each optimization step more expensive (Appendix [B.6](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#A2.SS6 "B.6 Time Complexity ‣ Appendix B Inference-time Steering of Video World Models ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement") for more details). However, random sampling still requires evaluating generated samples with expensive verifiers, so systematic steering within a finite sampling budget remains useful for discovering high-impact outcomes from WMs.

Reward Hacking. Although our gradient-based optimization with the Vision-Language-Model’s gradient is empirically effective, it can sometimes introduce reward hacking, where the criterion increases without inducing meaningful changes in the generated video [[34](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib20), [106](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib30), [55](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib125)]. Prior work mitigates this issue by combining multiple reward functions or adding image-/video-quality metrics that directly penalize degenerate generations [[34](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib20), [89](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib40)]. StressDream can also incorporate these strategies. In practice, however, we observe that VLM-based criteria trained on internet-scale data are substantially more robust than reward functions learned from scratch: they tend to assign high scores only when the target event is semantically evident in the generated video, whereas task-specific learned rewards are more susceptible to adversarial artifacts. This limitation may be further mitigated by more efficient video WM architectures with robust latent representations [[90](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib84)], shortcut/distilled diffusion models with fewer denoising steps [[47](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib85)], and stronger reward models with better video understanding and robustness to adversarial artifacts [[71](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib65)]. Moreover, StressDream requires specifying target high-impact outcomes with text prompts, which may need to be adapted for each scene, and the criterion’s effectiveness depends on prompt quality (see Appendix [B.3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#A2.SS3 "B.3 Vision-Language Models as General Inference-Time Criterion ‣ Appendix B Inference-time Steering of Video World Models ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement")).

heading_path: StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement
Abstract
chunks.text:
###### Abstract

Video world models (WMs) have shown promise for policy evaluation and improvement by imagining realistic future observations conditioned on ego-robot actions. While WMs can model distributions over futures, policy evaluation and improvement typically rely on nominal imaginations, which can miss high-impact outcomes of robot actions unless prohibitively many samples are drawn. To enable robust policy evaluation and improvement over WM imaginations, we propose StressDream, which steers imaginations toward high-impact yet plausible outcomes specified at inference time by optimizing the initial noise of diffusion-based WMs. However, optimizing high-dimensional noise is challenging: the optimization must reason about nuanced, scene-dependent target events in generated videos while avoiding out-of-distribution (OOD) noise that yields implausible imaginations. We address this with two complementary objectives: a semantic objective with a Vision-Language Model that provides informative gradients by reasoning about the generated video, and a plausibility objective that prevents the optimized noise from drifting OOD. With state-of-the-art video world models for autonomous driving and robotic manipulation, we show that StressDream effectively steers imaginations toward high-impact yet plausible outcomes specified by text at inference time, such as task failures, enabling robust policy evaluation and improvement by identifying actions whose plausible futures include undesirable outcomes.

Keywords: World Models, Inference-time Steering, Policy Learning and Evaluation

1 Introduction
chunks.text:
## 1 Introduction

Video world models (WMs), or learned simulators of physical environments, have attracted significant interest in robotics, promising policy evaluation and improvement with substantially less costly real-world interaction [[1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib103), [117](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib106), [78](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib115)]. At their core, video WMs are generative models, such as diffusion and flow matching [[52](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib53), [59](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib58), [73](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib55)], learning distributions over future observations conditioned on ego robot actions, and thereby capturing the inherent uncertainty of physical interactions or behaviors of other agents [[7](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib90), [17](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib75), [39](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib76), [61](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib112)] (top, Fig. ). For example, in robotic manipulation, dropping an open bag from high above the table may or may not cause its contents to spill, leading to either task success or failure; in autonomous driving, the same ego-vehicle decision can elicit qualitatively different outcomes depending on the responses of surrounding agents, such as braking or maintaining speed.

Despite learning rich distributions over future outcomes, policy evaluation and improvement with WMs typically rely on nominal imaginations [[17](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib75), [38](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib94), [42](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib108), [41](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib109)], which can under-explore the diverse outcomes they are trained to model. Naively sampling imaginations from WMs can easily miss critical outcomes without drawing prohibitively many samples, making it ill-suited to the role of WMs: exploring plausible, high-impact outcomes of robot actions for policy evaluation and improvement [[128](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib130), [91](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib110), [108](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib131), [99](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib111)], where plausibility refers to outcomes supported by the learned WM distribution. For example, when a manipulator drops an open bag from high above the table, the WM’s distribution may include outcomes both with and without spilling; in contrast, when the bag is placed close to the table, spilling may be unlikely or absent from the outcome distribution (bottom, Fig. ). The ability to imagine plausible, high-impact outcomes can therefore allow the latter action to be preferred during policy evaluation, while the former is downweighted or suppressed during policy improvement. This motivates the central question of our work:

How can we efficiently steer video world models at inference time to imagine plausible, high-impact outcomes for policy evaluation and improvement?

Our key idea is to optimize the initial noise of a diffusion-based WM, steering generation toward high-impact events specified at inference time (e.g., spills or collisions), within the distribution of plausible outcomes. The challenge, however, is to guide this optimization in extremely high-dimensional noise spaces (e.g., 11M dims [[38](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib94)]): the optimization must reason about nuanced, scene-dependent target events from generated videos, while naive optimization can easily push the initial noise into out-of-distribution (OOD) regions [[95](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib43), [106](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib30)], producing implausible videos. To address this, we propose StressDream, which combines a semantic objective, using a Vision-Language Model (VLM) that reasons about what happens in the generated video to guide generation toward target events, with a plausibility objective that keeps the optimized noise within the in-distribution region. Together, StressDream provides dense gradient signals for searching the high-dimensional noise space, while preserving plausibility of generations, enabling video WMs to explore plausible, high-impact outcome distributions for robust policy evaluation and improvement.

11

Statement of Contributions. We propose StressDream, a novel inference-time steering method for diffusion-based video world models. Our algorithm optimizes the high-dimensional Gaussian initial noise to steer generations toward high-impact outcomes while preserving plausibility. Through experiments, we show: (i) in controlled settings with access to the true system dynamics, StressDream steers WM imaginations toward target task-failure events only when such outcomes are plausible; (ii) on state-of-the-art video world models for autonomous driving [[38](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib94)] and robotic manipulation [[42](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib108)], StressDream enables robust policy evaluation by detecting high-impact outcomes, such as task failures, with substantially higher recall (54%→94%54\%\rightarrow 94\%); and (iii) this robust evaluation improves policy by promoting robust actions that avoid potential failures, increasing the success rate of a Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policy [[57](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib67)] (39%→71%39\%\rightarrow 71\%).

where the inner optimization chooses a Gaussian noise to steer the WM generation toward a worst-case plausible future that maximizes the criterion, while the outer optimization selects a robust action sequence that keeps the criterion low across plausible futures, even under worst-case outcomes. Various methods can be used for the outer optimization: 𝓐 m{\mathcal{A}} may be a discrete set in a sampling-based solver [[130](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib88)], or a continuous action space over which a policy is optimized [[41](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib109)]. However, solving the inner optimization is challenging, as it requires optimizing over a high-dimensional noise space.

𝓐 m{\mathcal{A}}

Steering Imagination via Inference-time Noise Optimization. Since the initial noise acts as a control variable for the generation of WMs (Sec. [2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#S2 "2 Background: Action-conditioned Video World Models ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement")), the goal of the inner optimization corresponds to steering the WM imagination toward a high-impact outcome that remains plausible under the learned model. However, because evaluating each noise requires an expensive denoising process, repeated random sampling is highly inefficient and likely to miss rare but plausible critical outcomes within a limited sampling budget. Instead, we leverage the gradient of a differentiable criterion function to steer generation more efficiently, optimizing the initial noise directly via gradient ascent:

Challenge: High-Dimensional Noise Space. While gradient-based optimization in ([5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#S3.E5 "In 3 Setup: Policy Evaluation and Improvement with Video World Models ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement")) can steer diffusion model generation at inference time [[106](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib30), [34](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib20)], applying it to video world models is challenging because their noise spaces are extremely high-dimensional, e.g., ≈1\approx 1M in driving [[38](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib94)] and ≈50\approx 50K in manipulation [[42](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib108)]. The optimization must guide generation toward meaningful, scene-dependent target events while preserving plausibility under the learned WM distribution. However, naive optimization can easily push the noise into out-of-distribution (OOD) regions of Gaussian noises, producing implausible videos (Fig. ), and the test-time criterion 𝒞test\mathcal{C}^{	ext{test}} must be differentiable while reasoning about nuanced, task-relevant events that vary across scenes. To make optimization efficient, we adopt a score-distillation [[3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib31)] (Appendix [B.4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#A2.SS4 "B.4 Score-Distillation for Approximating Initial-Noise Gradients ‣ Appendix B Inference-time Steering of Video World Models ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement")), which approximates the gradient with respect to the noise using the gradient at the generated sample:

StressDream reliably detects failures only when they are plausible. Fig. [1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#S5.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 5 Case Study: Steering Dubins Car Video World Model ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement") shows that StressDream accurately detects potential failures in WM imaginations, achieving a high true positive rate, i.e., correctly identifying trajectories that can fail, while maintaining a high true negative rate, i.e., not falsely classifying safe trajectories as failures. In contrast, StressDream without the plausibility objective in Sec. [4.2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#S4.SS2 "4.2 Plausibility Objective: Keeping High-dimensional Noise in the Typical Set ‣ 4 StressDream: Steering High-Dimensional Video World Models ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement") yields a low true-negative rate, indicating implausible failures are imagined without the typical set constraint. CG similarly produces many false positives by directly modifying the denoising trajectory, generating implausible imaginations. Random sampling methods (Nominal, Best-of-N) generate plausible imaginations, but are less effective at identifying rare possible failures compared to StressDream, often missing them even with multiple samples.

## 6 Experiments: Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement

In this section, we validate StressDream for robust policy evaluation and improvement using state-of-the-art video world models in both autonomous driving [[38](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib94)] and robotic manipulation [[42](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib108)].

Autonomous Driving. We use Vista [[38](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib94)] that predicts 2525 future front-view camera frames at 576×1024576\times 1024, conditioned on future waypoints as actions, with noise dimension D=921,600D=921{,}600. We fine-tune the model on the PhysicalAI-Autonomous-Vehicles (PAI-AV) dataset [[86](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib62)] and the Nexar Collision Prediction Dataset [[81](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib63)], which include diverse driving scenarios such as collisions. We optimize for 2020 steps with Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct [[10](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib52)] fine-tuned with Wolf [[67](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib97)] and X-CLIP [[76](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib64)].

We consider six contact-rich manipulation tasks (See Fig. [6](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#S6.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ 6.2 Policy Improvement with Steered Video World Model Imaginations ‣ 6 Experiments: Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement")) and collect approximately 150150 teleoperation trajectories per task containing both successes and failures to fine-tune the model. We optimize noise for 1010 steps using Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct [[9](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib50)], providing the three-view videos along with a prompt describing the task failure (More details in Appendix [D.1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#A4.SS1 "D.1 Video World Models ‣ Appendix D Experiment Details ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement")).

### 6.1 Robust Policy Evaluation using State-of-the-Art Video World Models

We first study whether StressDream enables robust policy evaluation by efficiently steering WM imaginations toward high-impact but plausible outcomes specified at inference time. As a baseline, we compare against random generation (Best-of-N), which samples multiple imaginations without optimization with the same budget as StressDream, and selects the one with the highest score.

𝒞pla\mathcal{C}^{\text{pla}}

Evaluation Setup. We generate imaginations from an initial observation o0o\_{0} and action sequence 𝐚\mathbf{a}, and evaluate whether the generated video matches the inference-time text specification 𝒍\bm{l} of the target event. For driving, we curate 100100 image–action–text pairs from the PAI-AV dataset [[86](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib62)] across 88 safety-critical event categories (see Appendix [D.3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#A4.SS3 "D.3 Autonomous Driving: Evaluation Data Curation ‣ Appendix D Experiment Details ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement")), as well as 200200 imminent-collision examples [[81](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib63)]. Each prompt describes a target event that has not yet occurred in the initial observation but occurs within the prediction horizon. For manipulation, we collect 100100 failure trajectories across tasks as an evaluation dataset, and evaluate whether WM imaginations from the initial images and the action sequences can reliably identify failures (See Appendix [D.2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#A4.SS2 "D.2 Robotic Manipulation: Task Details ‣ Appendix D Experiment Details ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement")).

Evaluation Metrics. For driving, we report target alignment and video quality using a held-out evaluator, WorldModelBench [[68](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib98)]. Target alignment measures whether the video matches the text description of the target event, while video quality serves as a proxy for plausibility. For manipulation, we label each generation as a success or failure based on human judgment. (See Appendix [D.4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#A4.SS4 "D.4 Evaluation Metrics ‣ Appendix D Experiment Details ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement"))

StressDream robustly detects high-impact outcomes in imaginations. Fig. [2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#S6.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 6.1 Robust Policy Evaluation using State-of-the-Art Video World Models ‣ 6 Experiments: Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement") compares nominal and steered generations. StressDream plausibly generates videos aligned with inference-time specifications of target safety-critical or failure events that nominal imaginations miss, enabling robust evaluation of action sequences through WM imaginations. Fig. [3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#S6.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 6.1 Robust Policy Evaluation using State-of-the-Art Video World Models ‣ 6 Experiments: Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement") shows that, without the typical-set constraint, both target-alignment and video-quality scores decrease, indicating that the plausibility objective helps preserve plausibility. For manipulation, StressDream detects task-failure events in imagination with higher recall, whereas random generations are often overly optimistic and miss possible failures, as shown in Fig. [4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#S6.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 6.1 Robust Policy Evaluation using State-of-the-Art Video World Models ‣ 6 Experiments: Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement"). More results in Appendix [E.1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#A5.SS1 "E.1 Robust Policy Evaluation via Video World Model Steering ‣ Appendix E Additional Results ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement") & [Website](https://stressdream.github.io/#policy-eval).

Steering is grounded in plausible outcomes. We study whether steering remains grounded in plausible outcomes supported by the WM’s distribution, rather than hallucinating implausible futures. To test this, we steer generations toward collision events using both the collision-finetuned Vista model and the base Vista model, which is not trained on collision events. Fig. [5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#S6.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 6.1 Robust Policy Evaluation using State-of-the-Art Video World Models ‣ 6 Experiments: Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement") shows that the base model cannot imagine collision outcomes even with steering, achieving lower target-alignment scores than random sampling from the collision-finetuned model. This indicates that StressDream steers only toward events supported by the WM outcome distribution, rather than synthesizing implausible events. Similarly, the right two columns of Fig. [2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#S6.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 6.1 Robust Policy Evaluation using State-of-the-Art Video World Models ‣ 6 Experiments: Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement") show that target spilling outcomes are induced only when plausible under the WM distribution: StressDream does not induce spilling for the open sticky candy bag or closed coffee bag, but does so for the open coffee bag. Since sticky candies are unlikely to spill and a closed bag does not expose its contents, spilling is not supported by the WM distribution in those scenes. More details and results in Appendix [E.3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#A5.SS3 "E.3 StressDream Steers into Plausible Outcomes Only ‣ Appendix E Additional Results ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement").
