7 Conclusion
chunks.text:
## 7 Conclusion

In this work, we propose StressDream, which steers video world model imaginations toward high-impact outcomes specified at inference-time, while remaining within the distribution of plausible outcomes. StressDream optimizes the high-dimensional initial noise of diffusion-based video world models using a combination of semantic and plausibility objectives: VLM gradients steer generation toward high-impact outcomes specified by inference-time prompts, while typical-set constraints keep the high-dimensional noise typical under the Gaussian prior. With WMs for autonomous driving and robotic manipulation, we demonstrate that StressDream effectively steers imaginations while preserving plausibility, enabling robust policy evaluation by identifying actions with potential failures and improving policies by favoring robust actions that avoid such failures.

Limitations. StressDream requires specifying high-impact outcomes with text descriptions, so its effectiveness depends on prompt quality and may suffer from reward hacking, where the score increases without meaningful changes in generations [[34](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib20), [55](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib125)], highlighting the need for generalizable and robust reward models for robotics [[105](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib129), [71](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib65)]. In addition, StressDream may fail to preserve plausibility or to discover relevant failures when the base WM is limited: it may steer within flawed videos produced by the WM, or fail to imagine target outcomes absent from the WM’s training distribution. Thus, our notion of plausibility is limited to what the WM supports, and does not necessarily imply physical plausibility in the real world, underscoring the need for diverse robot data to train high-fidelity WMs with physically consistent predictions. Runtime also remains expensive, as current WMs take several minutes per imagination [[38](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib94), [42](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib108)], though this could be reduced by efficient models [[102](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib126), [64](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib127), [32](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib128)]. We refer readers to Appendix [F](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#A6 "Appendix F Limitations & Discussions ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement") for a more detailed discussion.

### A.1 Related Works

World Models for Robotics. World models have emerged as a promising paradigm for robotics, enabling the prediction of future states directly from high-dimensional sensory observations conditioned on actions [[36](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib68), [31](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib69), [44](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib70), [122](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib83), [130](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib88), [79](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib89), [15](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib102), [1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib103), [77](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib87)]. By generating synthetic trajectories, they have proven effective for vision-based policy learning [[43](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib71), [45](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib72), [46](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib73), [47](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib85), [82](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib7), [2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib1), [99](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib111), [41](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib109)], planning in latent space [[130](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib88), [90](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib84)], and policy evaluation [[48](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib86), [42](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib108), [91](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib110)]. Advances in video generation models [[14](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib96)], which produce realistic and temporally consistent predictions, have further increased the expressiveness of world models in diverse real-world scenarios, especially when fine-tuned with embodiment data for action conditioning [[38](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib94), [50](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib95), [42](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib108)]. World models typically operate under partial observability, which naturally gives rise to uncertainty and multimodality in future predictions [[114](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib81), [129](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib74), [61](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib112)], particularly in settings such as contact-rich manipulation [[42](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib108)] or autonomous driving [[38](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib94), [94](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib82), [11](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib80), [50](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib95)]. In particular, diffusion- and flow-matching-based [[52](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib53), [59](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib58), [73](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib55)] approaches have shown strong performance in modeling high-dimensional, complex environments due to their ability to capture rich, multimodal distributions over future observations [[7](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib90), [17](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib75), [39](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib76), [61](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib112)]. Despite this, many existing methods using world models either rely on nominal rollouts without reasoning over distribution over plausible futures [[17](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib75), [42](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib108), [98](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib8)] or adopt deterministic world models that cannot represent such diversity [[130](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib88), [77](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib87)], thereby failing to explicitly account for risks arising from uncertain futures.

Inference-time Steering of Generative Models. Inference-time steering of diffusion [[52](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib53), [103](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib13)] or flow-matching [[73](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib55), [74](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib57)] model aims to guide a pretrained generative model toward samples that maximize an inference-time reward [[106](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib30), [110](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib12), [111](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib22), [54](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib28)]. While directly fine-tuning diffusion models with reward objectives can be effective for reward alignment [[35](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib36), [115](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib37), [89](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib40), [24](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib39), [110](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib12), [28](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib38)], it is costly, complex, tied to a specific reward [[106](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib30), [54](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib28)], and may shift the model away from the original data distribution [[33](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib29)]. In contrast, inference-time steering keeps the pretrained model fixed and instead modifies the sampling procedure [[23](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib10), [51](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib11), [106](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib30), [111](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib22), [100](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib24), [126](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib23)], for example through classifier guidance [[103](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib13)] or particle-based sampling methods such as Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) [[121](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib46), [29](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib47), [88](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib41), [54](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib28)]. One particularly relevant direction is noise optimization, which optimizes the noise sampled at the denoising process [[116](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib16), [40](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib26), [60](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib19), [34](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib20), [85](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib21), [106](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib30)]. Prior work has shown that this can improve image quality [[40](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib26), [18](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib25), [33](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib29)], mimic the effects of diffusion guidance [[3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib31)], generate rare [[95](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib43), [96](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib32), [97](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib33)] or diverse concepts [[63](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib34)], and adapt diffusion policies in robotic control [[113](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib35)]. However, a central challenge, especially when the noise space becomes high-dimensional, is out-of-distribution noise: samples may achieve high reward while no longer remaining in the support of the pretrained distribution once the noise deviates from the prior [[95](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib43), [12](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib44), [106](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib30), [34](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib20), [127](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib42), [33](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib29), [49](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib27)]. Moreover, these methods often require backpropagating reward gradients through the denoising process; in practice, many therefore rely on step-distilled models to make backpropagation tractable [[84](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib49), [34](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib20), [33](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib29), [27](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib48)], while recent works propose multistep score distillation to approximate reward gradients to the initial noise more efficiently [[3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib31)]. Our approach adopts initial noise optimization to steer action-conditioned video world models [[38](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib94), [42](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib108)] with a practical solution for high-dimensional noise optimization.

### A.3 Action-conditioned Video World Models

Video world models for robotics have shown promise for policy evaluation and improvement by simulating hard-to-model systems directly from high-dimensional sensor observations [[78](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib115)]. In robotic manipulation, for example, a world model can anticipate how objects may spill, slip, or topple during physical interaction from camera observations [[82](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib7), [98](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib8), [119](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib107)]. In autonomous driving, it can simulate future scene evolution in complex environments, capturing agent interactions and safety-critical situations directly in image space [[38](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib94), [50](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib95)]. These capabilities can support the evaluation and improvement of visuomotor control policies in simulation, reducing reliance on costly, time-consuming, and potentially unsafe real-world trials [[78](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib115), [125](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib105)].

Stable Video Diffusion. Recent video world models often build on video generation models [[1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib103), [117](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib106)], which have demonstrated strong ability to synthesize realistic and temporally coherent videos. Rather than learning from scratch, many recent approaches initialize from large-scale video diffusion models and then fine-tune them on domain-specific datasets such as driving or robotic manipulation. A widely used backbone is Stable Video Diffusion (SVD) [[14](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib96)], a latent diffusion model for image-to-video generation. SVD uses an encoder–decoder architecture to map RGB frames into a learned latent space, z=ℰ⁡(o)∈ℝ4×H/8×W/8,z=\mathcal{E}(o)\in\mathbb{R}^{4\times H/8\times W/8}, where HH and WW denote the image height and width. The diffusion model is then trained to denoise latent video representations, following an objective of the form in ([11](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#A1.E11 "In A.2 Diffusion Models ‣ Appendix A Background ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement")), and the generated latents are decoded back into RGB video frames using the decoder.

HH

WW

Action Conditioning. For robotic applications, video world models are conditioned on actions to enable controllable future generation [[38](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib94), [42](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib108)]. These actions may correspond to future ego-vehicle controls or trajectories in autonomous driving [[38](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib94), [50](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib95)], or to robot action sequences such as end-effector poses, joint-position commands, or low-level control commands in robotic manipulation [[42](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib108), [65](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib104)]. In the notation of ([11](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#A1.E11 "In A.2 Diffusion Models ‣ Appendix A Background ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement")), the denoiser is conditioned on histories and actions, gθτ​(𝐱τ,𝐨hist,𝐚),g^{\tau}\_{\theta}\left(\mathbf{x}^{\tau},\mathbf{o}^{\text{hist}},\mathbf{a}\right), so that the generated future is constrained to be consistent with both the observed history and the specified action sequence. While earlier world models often learned latent dynamics from task-specific observation–action trajectories [[43](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib71), [46](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib73), [48](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib86)], recent diffusion-based video world models built on SVD typically start from a pretrained video diffusion model and post-train it with action-conditioned data. When trained with conditional dropout, these models can also use classifier-free guidance at sampling time to trade off visual realism and action controllability [[53](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib14)].

History Conditioning. To generate coherent future frames that remain consistent with the conditioning observations, recent video world models incorporate observation history in several ways. Some methods inject conditioning frames by replacing the corresponding noisy latent frames with clean observed latents during sampling [[38](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib94)]; others use progressive or autoregressive sampling with per-frame noise schedules to encourage causal structure across time [[17](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib75), [50](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib95)]; and some provide sparse history frames or memory tokens as additional network inputs through attention-based conditioning [[42](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib108)]. These mechanisms help preserve temporal continuity, keep generated futures consistent with the observed history, supporting longer-horizon, autoregressive video generation by conditioning future predictions on previous observations or generated frames.

Application: Policy Evaluation & Improvement. Action-conditioned video world models can support robot learning without repeated real-world rollouts, enabling scalable data generation, planning, policy evaluation, and policy improvement. Because current state-of-the-art video generation models are often slow and memory-intensive, they are typically used offline rather than for real-time planning. Prior work has primarily leveraged action-conditioned video prediction in two ways: (i) using imagined rollouts to evaluate or optimize policies without repeated hardware trials [[91](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib110), [42](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib108), [109](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib77), [70](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib78), [125](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib105)], and (ii) generating synthetic trajectories for data augmentation or policy fine-tuning [[42](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib108), [58](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib79), [99](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib111), [41](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib109), [125](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib105)]. In particular, recent works report that video world models can serve as simulators for closed-loop evaluation of visuomotor policies, with predicted performance correlating with real-world success rates [[42](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib108)]. Similarly, policies can be improved using video world models, either through reinforcement learning inside imagined rollouts [[99](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib111)] or by searching for successful synthetic trajectories that are then used to fine-tune the policy [[41](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib109)].

While our method can be applied to these broader settings, our experiments focus specifically on the value of steering video world models for robust policy evaluation and improvement. Rather than evaluating a complete robotic policy in a closed loop, we evaluate candidate trajectories that could be produced by a policy and assess their potential failure risks. Similarly, rather than improving policies through closed-loop exploration inside the world model, we use the steered world model to identify failure-prone expert trajectories and reweight them during policy fine-tuning.

### B.1 Regularizing Noise within the Typical Set of High-Dimensional Gaussian Distribution

In this section, we elaborate on Sec. [4.2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#S4.SS2 "4.2 Plausibility Objective: Keeping High-dimensional Noise in the Typical Set ‣ 4 StressDream: Steering High-Dimensional Video World Models ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement"), where we impose typical-set constraints during noise optimization. In high-dimensional Gaussian distributions, regions of high probability density do not necessarily coincide with regions of high probability mass, where typical samples concentrate. For example, the zero vector has the highest density under a standard Gaussian, yet it is almost never sampled in high dimensions; instead, typical samples lie on a thin shell with squared norm approximately dd. We refer to this high-mass region as the typical set. As illustrated in Fig. [8](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#A2.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ B.1 Regularizing Noise within the Typical Set of High-Dimensional Gaussian Distribution ‣ Appendix B Inference-time Steering of Video World Models ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement"), the typical set is distinct from the high-density region, and sampling noise outside the typical set can lead to implausible generations. This distinction is important for diffusion models, which are trained to denoise samples initialized from typical Gaussian noise. If optimization pushes the initial noise toward atypical, low-mass regions of the prior, the denoiser may be evaluated on inputs rarely seen during training, leading to approximation errors and, consequently, implausible or OOD generations.

dd

A common way to encourage typicality is to regularize the norm of the optimized noise, since Gaussian samples exhibit strong norm concentration in high dimensions. Several prior methods have found norm-based regularization sufficient for preserving plausibility in diffusion generation [[95](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib43), [34](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib20), [106](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib30)]. However, the norm captures only one of the numerous sample statistics of a Gaussian sample. In practice, we find that additional typicality constraints are important for high-dimensional video world models. Thus, as described in Sec. [4.2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#S4.SS2 "4.2 Plausibility Objective: Keeping High-dimensional Noise in the Typical Set ‣ 4 StressDream: Steering High-Dimensional Video World Models ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement"), we regularize multiple statistics of the optimized noise, including norm concentration, isotropy, and spectral whiteness, each motivated by concentration properties of high-dimensional Gaussian samples.

Fig. [9](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#A2.F9 "Figure 9 ‣ B.1 Regularizing Noise within the Typical Set of High-Dimensional Gaussian Distribution ‣ Appendix B Inference-time Steering of Video World Models ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement") illustrates examples of Gaussian noise visualized as 2D images, where each atypical sample violates one statistic of the Gaussian typical set. Violating norm concentration produces noise with globally biased values compared to typical Gaussian noise. Violating isotropy introduces local coordinate patterns that do not appear in typical i.i.d. noise, while violating spectral whiteness produces structured, non-white patterns in the frequency domain.

Thus, a large value indicates an atypical spatial frequency structure. This regularizer is complementary to isotropy: isotropy checks covariance after random coordinate grouping, whereas spectral whiteness checks whether energy is evenly distributed across spatial frequencies.

### B.3 Vision-Language Models as General Inference-Time Criterion

Rather than learning a task-specific reward function or failure classifier for a narrow set of events [[82](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib7), [98](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib8)], we use a VLM as an inference-time verifier that can flexibly specify steering targets across diverse scenes and event categories [[123](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib117)]. This is particularly useful for general-purpose video world models, whose possible futures may vary widely with the scene and action context.

VLMs also provide semantically meaningful gradient signals: task-specific reward models trained on limited datasets may fail to cover the large space of possible video generations, making them vulnerable to reward hacking [[24](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib39), [34](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib20)], where optimization increases the reward through adversarial or visually meaningless changes rather than by producing the intended event. In contrast, because VLMs are trained on large-scale vision-language data, they can provide a more general semantic signal for whether the generated video depicts the specified event [[120](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib118)].

Since our method relies on dense gradient signals from VLMs, we use open-source models rather than API-based evaluators [[107](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib66)], despite the strong scene-understanding capabilities of recent proprietary models. We adopt different VLMs for autonomous driving and robotic manipulation based on the semantic structure of each domain.

Autonomous Driving. In autonomous driving, the target events we aim to steer often depend on temporal relationships among agents, such as pedestrian motion, vehicle movement, or changes in relative distance. We empirically find that off-the-shelf Qwen models [[8](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib51)] are less reliable at understanding driving scenes and their temporal structure. We therefore use the Qwen2.5-VL model fine-tuned on autonomous driving videos by [67](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib97), which provides improved driving-scene understanding. We also use X-CLIP [[76](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib64)], which we find effective at capturing temporal relationships. As shown in Fig. [10](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#A2.F10 "Figure 10 ‣ B.3 Vision-Language Models as General Inference-Time Criterion ‣ Appendix B Inference-time Steering of Video World Models ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement"), for three generated videos where the relative distance to the lead vehicle is increasing, unchanged, or decreasing, both the fine-tuned Qwen model and X-CLIP [[76](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib64)] assign scores that correctly distinguish these cases. For CLIP-style models, we define a positive prompt 𝒍+\bm{l}\_{+} and a negative prompt 𝒍−\bm{l}\_{-}. We embed both prompts and the generated video into the shared embedding space, and use the difference in cosine similarities as the steering objective:

𝒍+\bm{l}_{+}

𝒍−\bm{l}_{-}

| | | | | --- | --- | --- | | | 𝒞sem​(𝐨)=sim⁡(evideo​(𝐨),etext​(𝒍+))−sim⁡(evideo​(𝐨),etext​(𝒍−)).\mathcal{C}^{\text{sem}}(\mathbf{o})=\mathrm{sim}\!\left(e^{\text{video}}(\mathbf{o}),e^{\text{text}}(\bm{l}\_{+})\right)-\mathrm{sim}\!\left(e^{\text{video}}(\mathbf{o}),e^{\text{text}}(\bm{l}\_{-})\right). | |

𝒞sem​(𝐨)=sim⁡(evideo​(𝐨),etext​(𝒍+))−sim⁡(evideo​(𝐨),etext​(𝒍−)).\mathcal{C}^{\text{sem}}(\mathbf{o})=\mathrm{sim}\!\left(e^{\text{video}}(\mathbf{o}),e^{\text{text}}(\bm{l}_{+})\right)-\mathrm{sim}\!\left(e^{\text{video}}(\mathbf{o}),e^{\text{text}}(\bm{l}_{-})\right).

Robotic Manipulation. In tabletop manipulation, our steering objective focuses on detecting task-failure events from generated videos. We use Qwen3-VL [[9](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib50)] with a text prompt that defines the failure condition, and compute the score from the token probability of the target response, similar to recent generalizable reward-modeling approaches [[19](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib119)]. Fig. [11](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#A2.F11 "Figure 11 ‣ B.3 Vision-Language Models as General Inference-Time Criterion ‣ Appendix B Inference-time Steering of Video World Models ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement") shows that the model score identifies task-relevant events at the correct moments in generated videos. We provide the five-frame videos generated by the world model as input and backpropagate dense gradient signals through the video. We find that using all three camera views simultaneously is essential for reliable scoring: for the same scene and text prompt, using a single viewpoint leads to substantially poorer failure-event detection. We also find that CLIP-style models, including X-CLIP [[76](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib64)], are less effective at understanding these manipulation scenes.

Our approximation uses this same principle, but applies it directly to optimize the initial noise: the clean-latent criterion gradient is used as a proxy direction for the initial-noise gradient, with the unknown scalar absorbed into β\beta and the learning rate.

β\beta

Efficacy of Gradient Approximation for Noise Optimization. The noise-gradient approximation enables efficient gradient-based steering without backpropagating through the iterative denoising process of large-scale video diffusion models. However, it relies on the assumption that the Jacobian of the diffusion sampler is approximately diagonal [[3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib31)]. Indeed, prior work on noise optimization for text-to-image generation often relies on one-step distilled generators to make noise optimization tractable without differentiating through the full iterative sampling process.

We therefore empirically evaluate whether this approximation provides a useful gradient signal in the initial-noise space for generating high-reward samples in the output space. Fig. [12](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#A2.F12 "Figure 12 ‣ B.4 Score-Distillation for Approximating Initial-Noise Gradients ‣ Appendix B Inference-time Steering of Video World Models ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement") shows the average VLM score during noise optimization for steering Vista [[38](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib94)] generations in Sec. [6.1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#S6.SS1 "6.1 Robust Policy Evaluation using State-of-the-Art Video World Models ‣ 6 Experiments: Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement"). The score increases throughout optimization, indicating that the approximate gradient can improve the output-space VLM objective by updating only the initial noise. On an H100 GPU with 8080GB VRAM, computing the full gradient through the denoising trajectory is impractical even with gradient checkpointing [[21](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib116)], whereas the proposed approximation makes the optimization feasible.

8080

For Ctrl-World [[42](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib108)], where the full noise gradient can be computed on an H100 GPU using gradient checkpointing [[21](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib116)], we compare noise optimization with and without the gradient approximation. Fig. [13](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#A2.F13 "Figure 13 ‣ B.4 Score-Distillation for Approximating Initial-Noise Gradients ‣ Appendix B Inference-time Steering of Video World Models ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement") shows that the approximate gradient successfully increases the VLM score, whereas optimization with the full gradient fails to improve it. We hypothesize two possible causes. First, backpropagating through 5050 denoising steps may lead to inaccurate or vanishing gradients due to finite-precision computation. Second, while the VLM gradient is computed in the video space with relatively high numerical precision, the denoising process is typically run in lower precision due to memory constraints, which may further degrade gradient quality.

### C.2 Ablation: Optimistic Steering

While Sec. [5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#S5 "5 Case Study: Steering Dubins Car Video World Model ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement") focuses on pessimistic steering to detect potential entries into the failure set, we also ablate the opposite direction by performing optimistic steering. Specifically, we change the sign of the steering objective so that optimization seeks imaginations with higher safety scores. Fig. [15](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#A3.F15 "Figure 15 ‣ C.2 Ablation: Optimistic Steering ‣ Appendix C Naughty Dubins Car ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement") shows the resulting maximum safety score for each imagined trajectory, together with the maximum safety score achievable under the ground-truth stochastic dynamics as a horizontal reference line. The results are consistent with the findings in Sec. [5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#S5 "5 Case Study: Steering Dubins Car Video World Model ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement"): StressDream can steer the world model effectively, here toward optimistic outcomes, while keeping the generated trajectories plausibly bounded by the ground-truth uncertainty. In contrast, removing the regularizers or using classifier guidance can also increase the imagined safety score, but often produces overly optimistic generations that exceed what is plausible under the ground-truth system dynamics.

StressDream with all regularizers keeps the noise statistics close to nominal generation while maintaining a low OOD score. In contrast, steering without regularization produces highly atypical noise and substantially larger OOD scores, suggesting that the optimized generations leave the training distribution. Classifier guidance keeps the initial noise statistics close to nominal because it modifies the denoising trajectory rather than the initial noise, but it still increases the OOD score, indicating that path-level guidance can push generated samples toward implausible regions. ### D.2 Robotic Manipulation: Task Details

We describe the manipulation task setups, the criteria used to determine success or failure, and the language prompts used for steering the generated futures. Visual examples of the task setups are shown in Fig. [6](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#S6.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ 6.2 Policy Improvement with Steered Video World Model Imaginations ‣ 6 Experiments: Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement") and on the [project website](https://stressdream.github.io/).

Block Stack. Two Jenga blocks, one orange and one blue, are placed on the table. The robot is tasked with stacking the orange block on top of the blue block. A trajectory is considered a success if the orange block remains on top of the blue block, and a failure if the robot fails to stack the block or if the orange block falls off after stacking. VLM prompt: Are the two blocks stacked? Respond with a single word: Yes or No.

Knife Put. A lightweight plastic bowl and a knife are placed on the table. The robot is tasked with picking up the knife and placing it inside the bowl without causing either object to fall. This task is challenging because the knife has an uneven center of mass and a complex shape, while the lightweight bowl can easily tip over. A trajectory is considered a success if the knife is placed inside the bowl and remains there, and a failure if the knife falls out or the bowl tips over. VLM prompt: Is the knife placed inside of the blue bowl without falling out? Respond with a single word: Yes or No.

Stacked Utensil Pick. A blue knife and a red spoon are overlapped on a green plate, with the red spoon placed on top of the blue knife. The robot is instructed to pick up the blue knife while keeping the red spoon on the plate. A trajectory is considered a success if the blue knife is successfully picked up and the spoon remains on the plate, and a failure if the blue knife is not picked up or if the spoon falls off the plate. The robot should therefore remove the lower utensil while safely leaving the upper utensil on the plate. VLM prompt: Is the red spoon in the green plate? Respond with a single word: Yes or No.

Coffee Bean Pour. A bowl is on top of a coffee scale, and a cup contains coffee beans. The robot is tasked with pouring the coffee beans from the cup into the bowl on the scale. A trajectory is considered a success if the coffee beans are poured into the bowl without spilling, and a failure if any coffee beans spill onto the table. VLM prompt: Is the coffee bean spilled on the table? Respond with a single word: Yes or No.

Open Coffee Bag. An open coffee bag with a variable and partially unobservable amount of coffee beans inside is on the table, along with a container. The robot is instructed to place the coffee bag inside the container. A trajectory is considered a failure if any coffee beans spill out of the bag, either into the container or onto the table. Thus, the robot must avoid spilling while lifting, carrying, and placing the bag into the container. VLM prompt: Is the coffee bean spilled? Respond with a single word: Yes or No.

Open Candy Bag. An open gummy bear candy bag is on the table, and the robot is instructed to place it inside the container without spilling. Compared to coffee beans, gummy bears are stickier and heavier, creating a smaller risk of spilling out of the bag. A trajectory is considered a success if the gummy bears remain inside the bag, and a failure if any gummy bears spill out. VLM prompt: Does candy spill from an open bag? Respond with a single word: Yes or No.

### D.3 Autonomous Driving: Evaluation Data Curation

To evaluate steering for autonomous driving video world models, we curate an evaluation set from the PAI-AV dataset [[86](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib62)]. We focus on scenarios in which the future evolution is uncertain or interaction-dependent, such as pedestrian crossing, vehicle merging, traffic-light changes, and stop-sign behavior. Table [8](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#A4.T8 "Table 8 ‣ D.3 Autonomous Driving: Evaluation Data Curation ‣ Appendix D Experiment Details ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement") summarizes the event categories and the verifier prompts used for Qwen-VL [[8](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib51)] and X-CLIP [[76](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib64)]. For X-CLIP, the first text description is treated as the positive event description, while the remaining descriptions are used as negative alternatives.

To retrieve candidate clips from the large-scale dataset, we first extract VLM reasoning traces from Alpamayo-R1 [[118](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib61)] on PAI-AV clips. We then embed these traces using Sentence-BERT [[93](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib60)] and retrieve the top-kk clips whose embeddings are most similar to text descriptions of each event category. Human annotators then verify whether the target event occurs in each retrieved clip and label the event occurrence time. Since the video world model generates 2.52.5s futures, we select the frame 2.52.5s before the annotated event time as the initial observation for evaluation. We similarly curate an evaluation set of 200200 collision clips from the Nexar Collision Prediction Dataset [[81](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib63)] by randomly sampling from the provided collision annotations.

### D.4 Evaluation Metrics

Autonomous Driving. To evaluate steering, we use held-out metrics that are not used during optimization. This is important because a steered generation can increase the optimization score without producing a meaningful or plausible change in the video. We therefore evaluate two complementary aspects: (i) target alignment, i.e., whether the generated video clearly depicts the target event described by the text prompt, and (ii) plausibility, i.e., whether the generated video remains physically reasonable and free from severe visual artifacts that indicate out-of-distribution generation.

For autonomous driving, we adopt WorldModelBench (WMB) [[68](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib98)], which evaluates video world-model generations using both text-prompt alignment and video-quality criteria. We use WMB because it includes driving data in its evaluation distribution and, empirically, provides meaningful scores for whether generated driving videos both match the target prompt and remain visually plausible. WMB reports three scores: instruction following (0​–​3)(0\text{--}3), physics adherence (0​–​5)(0\text{--}5), and commonsense consistency (0​–​2)(0\text{--}2). We use the instruction-following score to measure target alignment, and use physics adherence and commonsense consistency as proxies for generation plausibility.

(0​–​3)(0\text{--}3)

(0​–​5)(0\text{--}5)

(0​–​2)(0\text{--}2)

In addition, we report a target-alignment score from an external VLM judge. This judge is used only for evaluation and is not used during steering. We use the following prompt template with Gemini [[107](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib66)] to obtain a 0​–​100\text{--}10 alignment score:

0​–​100\text{--}10

You are an expert evaluator of autonomous driving world models. Your ONLY task is to judge how well the video follows the text instruction. Ignore visual quality issues such as blur, flickering, warping, or low resolution: these are expected artifacts of world-model generation and must NOT affect your score.

TEXT DESCRIPTION: {prompt}

SCORING RUBRIC (0-10):

10: The video is aligned with the text description clearly and completely.

7-9: The video is aligned with the text description but with minor deviations (e.g., slightly wrong direction or timing).

4-6: The video is vaguely related to the text description, but the specific action does not happen.

1-3: The video is completely unrelated to the text description.

0: The video content is completely unrelated to the text description.

Robotic Manipulation. We use human evaluation to determine whether each generated trajectory corresponds to task success or failure. We additionally report scores from Robometer [[71](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib65)], a general-purpose robotic reward model. However, we rely on human evaluation as the primary metric for a more accurate assessment of generated trajectories, since reward models provide continuous scores and require prompt engineering to infer task success.

chunks.text:
### E.1 Robust Policy Evaluation via Video World Model Steering

In this section, we provide additional results for Sec. [6.1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#S6.SS1 "6.1 Robust Policy Evaluation using State-of-the-Art Video World Models ‣ 6 Experiments: Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement"). The evaluation focuses on steering video world-model generations toward text-defined failure events in each scene, enabling robust evaluation of policy-proposed action sequences through pessimistic world-model imaginations. We measure both target alignment, i.e., how well the generated videos match the failure prompt, and plausibility, i.e., whether the generations remain visually and physically reasonable. Full results, including videos and interactive demos, are available on the [project website](https://stressdream.github.io/).

Robust Policy Evaluation with Pessimistic Imaginations. Fig. [16](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#A5.F16 "Figure 16 ‣ E.1 Robust Policy Evaluation via Video World Model Steering ‣ Appendix E Additional Results ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement") shows additional results for the inner optimization in ([4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#S3.E4 "In 3 Setup: Policy Evaluation and Improvement with Video World Models ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement")) on robotic manipulation tasks. For the same observation history and action sequence, nominal imaginations often do not predict failure events, whereas StressDream generates plausible task-failure futures from the same input. This enables robust policy evaluation using the video world model by detecting possible failures through synthetic trajectories, without requiring repeated hardware rollouts. In contrast, nominal generation may miss such failures because it can sample non-failing futures even when failure is possible. Similarly, Fig. [17](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#A5.F17 "Figure 17 ‣ E.1 Robust Policy Evaluation via Video World Model Steering ‣ Appendix E Additional Results ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement") shows that, across different candidate action sequences, StressDream with pessimistic steering can reveal potential failures or safety-critical events in the imagined futures, while robust action sequences remain safe even under pessimistic imagination. This supports robust evaluation and action selection by using the video world model as a predictive model for planning and control.

Detailed Results: Driving Video World Model. Fig. [18](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#A5.F18 "Figure 18 ‣ E.1 Robust Policy Evaluation via Video World Model Steering ‣ Appendix E Additional Results ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement") shows the full quantitative results for driving world-model [[38](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib94)] steering, evaluated with WorldModelBench (WMB) [[68](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib98)] and Gemini-3.0 [[107](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib66)]. The top two plots measure target alignment between the generated videos and the steering text prompts, while the bottom two plots report WMB video-quality metrics. Across both alignment metrics, StressDream with noise optimization more effectively increases target-event alignment scores than the baselines with random generation, indicating that the proposed steering procedure reliably guides video world-model generation toward the desired events. At the same time, the proposed typical set constraint helps maintain plausibility: although video quality slightly decreases at later optimization steps, ours consistently preserves better quality in both common sense scores and physical laws scores than steering without regularization.

Typical Set Constraints Preserve Plausibility of Steered Video Generations. We have evaluated the plausibility of steered generations on VLM-based scores, such as the commonsense and physical-law scores in WorldModelBench [[68](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib98)]. To further assess the role of the plausibility objective in Sec. [4.2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#S4.SS2 "4.2 Plausibility Objective: Keeping High-dimensional Noise in the Typical Set ‣ 4 StressDream: Steering High-Dimensional Video World Models ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement"), we additionally evaluate generated driving videos using WorldLens [[72](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib99)]. We focus on generation-quality metrics that assess whether generated videos are visually realistic, temporally stable, and semantically consistent, without requiring multi-view images or ground-truth labels. Unlike VLM-based scores, these metrics are computed from analytic feature-based measures44 4 WorldLens also introduces a learned video score trained from large-scale human annotations of world realism, physical plausibility, and behavioral safety; however, since this model is not yet released..

Specifically, we evaluate Subject Consistency, Depth Discrepancy, and Temporal Consistency. Subject Consistency uses DINO features [[87](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib91)] to measure whether dynamic subjects maintain consistent texture, shape, and structure over time. Depth Discrepancy measures the temporal stability of depth representations inferred from generated videos using DepthAnything [[20](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib93)]. Temporal Consistency measures frame-to-frame stability in a learned appearance space using CLIP encodings [[92](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib92)]. We refer readers to the appendix of WorldLens [[72](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib99)] for detailed metric definitions. Fig. [19](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#A5.F19 "Figure 19 ‣ E.1 Robust Policy Evaluation via Video World Model Steering ‣ Appendix E Additional Results ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement") shows the WorldLens generation-quality scores for driving world-model generations. Consistent with the WMB video-quality metrics, generation quality tends to degrade at later noise-optimization steps. However, using the proposed typical set constraints substantially mitigates this degradation, preserving subject consistency, depth stability, and temporal consistency compared to steering without regularization.

Detailed Results: Failure Detection in Robotic Manipulation. Fig. [21](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#A5.F21 "Figure 21 ‣ E.1 Robust Policy Evaluation via Video World Model Steering ‣ Appendix E Additional Results ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement") reports task-wise failure-detection results for robotic manipulation video world models. Steering is performed using Qwen3-VL [[9](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib50)] scores computed from task-failure prompts, while the detection results are evaluated against trajectory-level success and failure labels from the dataset. Across tasks, StressDream detects substantially more failure-prone trajectories than nominal generation or Best-of-NN sampling.

NN

Fig. [21](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#A5.F21 "Figure 21 ‣ E.1 Robust Policy Evaluation via Video World Model Steering ‣ Appendix E Additional Results ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement") also shows that StressDream sometimes predicts failures for trajectories labeled as non-failure in the dataset. This should not be interpreted strictly as a false-positive rate: a trajectory that succeeded during data collection may still be risky under unobserved factors in a partially observable setting. Qualitatively, many of these flagged trajectories correspond to risky behaviors, suggesting that pessimistic imagination provides a more robust way of evaluating policies. At the same time, StressDream does not flag all non-failure trajectories as failures, indicating that the method can still identify robust trajectories that remain safe even under pessimistic world-model imagination. These robust trajectories can then be prioritized for policy improvement, rather than relying on demonstrations that may have succeeded only by chance.

### E.2 StressDream Can Effectively Discover Rare, Long-Tailed Events

Our main experiments evaluate whether StressDream can generate videos that satisfy an inference-time specification while preserving plausibility more effectively than random sampling. This is particularly important for video world models, which operate in high-dimensional spaces where targeted generation is difficult: rare events often occupy complex, multimodal, and low-probability regions of the generative distribution, making random sampling highly sample-inefficient. In this section, we ask a complementary question: can StressDream effectively discover rare events in the target distribution by optimizing the initial noise with VLM guidance?

To evaluate this, we sample 55 evaluation examples from long-tailed driving events in the evaluation set, including pedestrian crossing, traffic-light change, and collision. As a baseline, we generate 4040 random samples and report the best result among them, while StressDream performs 2020 optimization steps. We evaluate target alignment scores of generated videos using Gemini-3.0 [[107](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#bib.bib66)]. Fig. [22](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#A5.F22 "Figure 22 ‣ E.2 StressDream Can Effectively Discover Rare, Long-Tailed Events ‣ Appendix E Additional Results ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement") shows that StressDream is more effective at discovering rare events than random sampling. Even with 4040 samples, Best-of-NN sampling does not match the target-alignment score achieved by StressDream. This suggests that first-order optimization in the high-dimensional noise space can discover rare, long-tailed events more efficiently than zeroth-order search through random sampling.

### E.3 StressDream Steers into Plausible Outcomes Only

We further elaborate on the experiments in Sec. [6.1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#S6.SS1 "6.1 Robust Policy Evaluation using State-of-the-Art Video World Models ‣ 6 Experiments: Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement") by examining whether steered generations remain grounded in plausible outcomes of the world model. In particular, we compare a driving world model fine-tuned with collision data against the base model without such fine-tuning. As shown in Fig. [5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#S6.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 6.1 Robust Policy Evaluation using State-of-the-Art Video World Models ‣ 6 Experiments: Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement"), the base model yields low text–video alignment scores for collision events, even compared to random sampling from the collision-fine-tuned model, because collisions are not represented in its predictive distribution and therefore cannot be plausibly imagined.

Fig. [23](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#A5.F23 "Figure 23 ‣ E.3 StressDream Steers into Plausible Outcomes Only ‣ Appendix E Additional Results ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement") shows a qualitative example of imagination near a collision event using the base model and the collision-fine-tuned model. The base model fails to imagine the collision and instead hallucinates the other vehicle disappearing from the scene. In contrast, the fine-tuned model, whose predictive distribution includes collision events, correctly imagines the collision. This supports our claim that when the optimized noise remains close to the Gaussian prior, steering produces samples that are still supported by the world model distribution, rather than arbitrary hallucinations. In this sense, noise optimization differs from simply forcing inference-time alignment through a classifier or a fine-tuning objective, which can more easily push the generation off-manifold.

Similarly, Fig. [24](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2606.00267v1#A5.F24 "Figure 24 ‣ E.3 StressDream Steers into Plausible Outcomes Only ‣ Appendix E Additional Results ‣ StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement") shows an example of steering a driving WM generation so that the distance between the ego vehicle and the lead vehicle decreases. In the initial generation, the lead vehicle moves forward, roughly maintaining its distance from the ego vehicle. In the steered generation, the lead vehicle instead remains stopped while the ego vehicle continues moving, causing the distance to decrease. Although the distance could be reduced even further if the lead vehicle moved backward, such behavior is highly implausible in a normal driving scenario. Accordingly, the steered generation chooses the plausible outcome of the lead vehicle stopping, rather than the implausible outcome of it reversing. By contrast, when steering is performed without the plausibility objective, the generation hallucinates unrealistic artifacts, such as the distorted backward motion of vehicle shapes.
